passage:
Subject: Handing you the volunteer roster

Dear Salma,

I'd like you to own the volunteer roster for the June camp. The goal is that every shift has at least two people and nobody is asked to work two evenings in a row. It matters because last year we lost three volunteers who were overworked. The final roster is due on the 20th, and I'd like it to be clear enough to print. Use whatever tool suits you. Let's talk for ten minutes on the 12th, so I can see where you are.

Thursday: Thank you for the draft on the 12th. Your colour-coded grid is clearer than mine would have been, and I've asked for nothing to change.

Sudha

qa.q: By what date is the final roster due?
qa.a: The final roster is due on the 20th.

qa.q: Why does Sudha say the roster matters?
qa.a: Sudha explains that last year the camp lost three volunteers who were overworked, so the roster protects people from overload.

qa.q: What parts of the handover made the delegation work?
qa.a: Sudha stated the goal, the reason, the deadline and the quality expected, agreed a checkpoint on the 12th and let Salma choose the tool.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt receiving the email?
qa.a: Salma probably felt trusted and clear about what was wanted, and free to use Salma's own method, which likely made the work easier.

grounding: A wise delegator explains the goal, why it matters, the deadline and quality, agrees a checkpoint and lets the person choose the method.

passage:
Hemant: What's your rule for handing work to someone?
Manoj: I say four things. What the finished thing should do. Why it matters. When it's due. And what good looks like. Last month I gave a junior the monthly stock summary like that: a one-page table, so the shop owners can order on Monday, due Friday noon, with last month's version as the example. Then we agreed to meet on Wednesday for ten minutes. How he did it was up to him. He came on Wednesday with a draft I wouldn't have thought of, cleaner than mine. On Friday it was done, early. And I hadn't checked once in between.

qa.q: What day did Manoj and the junior agree to meet?
qa.a: They agreed to meet on Wednesday for ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel when the junior arrived on Wednesday with a draft?
qa.a: Manoj felt pleased and a little surprised: the draft was cleaner than Manoj's own and used a method Manoj wouldn't have thought of.

qa.q: What four things does Manoj say when handing over work?
qa.a: Manoj says what the finished thing should do, why it matters, when it is due, and what good looks like.

qa.q: How might the junior have felt about being trusted with the method?
qa.a: The junior probably felt trusted and motivated, since the method was left open, and finished early.

grounding: A wise delegator explains the goal, why it matters, the deadline and quality, agrees a check-in and allows the person their own method.

passage: I sit across from Chaitanya at the architecture firm, so I heard how he handed Vinita her first solo project last week. He didn't just say "do the site plan". He said the client, a small school, needed a drawing for their funding application. He explained why it mattered: without it, the school couldn't apply this year. The deadline was the 20th, and it had to be neat enough for a government office, not a competition. Then he said, "Let's look at a rough version on Tuesday. How you draw it is up to you." Vinita asked two questions and got started. On Tuesday her draft was already close. I can't know what she felt, but she looked quietly proud walking back to her desk.

qa.q: Who was the client for Vinita's site plan?
qa.a: The client was a small school.

qa.q: What might Vinita have felt walking back from the Tuesday check?
qa.a: She looked quietly proud, likely feeling trusted and confident after her draft was already close.

qa.q: Which parts of Chaitanya's handover made it work?
qa.a: He gave the goal, why it mattered, the deadline, the quality expected and one checkpoint, then let Vinita choose her method.

qa.q: How does the colleague who sits across from Chaitanya see the handover?
qa.a: The colleague sees it as unusually clear and respectful, noticing both the details given and the freedom left to Vinita.

grounding: An observer describes a lead delegating with goal, reason, deadline, standard and one checkpoint, while leaving the method free.

passage:
Monday. Harsha, twenty-six, managed the front desk at a busy hotel in Jaipur. He asked Sumit, a new staff member, to prepare the welcome kits for a wedding group of eighty guests. He explained: the group arrives Thursday, the kits make the first impression, each needs a map, a schedule and a water bottle, and they should look neat, not fancy. "Show me three finished kits on Tuesday evening. After that, your way."
Tuesday. Sumit showed three kits. One map was folded wrong. Harsha pointed it out and left.
Thursday. Eighty kits lined the desk, with a small handwritten note in each that Sumit had added himself. The guests loved the notes. Harsha hadn't thought of that.

qa.q: How many guests were in the wedding group?
qa.a: There were eighty guests.

qa.q: What might Sumit have felt when he added the handwritten notes?
qa.a: He likely felt trusted and confident enough to add his own idea, since the method was left to him.

qa.q: Which parts of Harsha's delegation helped?
qa.a: He explained the goal, why it mattered, the deadline, the quality expected and a Tuesday checkpoint, then stepped back.

qa.q: How does Harsha feel when the guests love the notes?
qa.a: Harsha is pleasantly surprised and likely proud, seeing that giving freedom produced an idea he hadn't thought of.

grounding: Shows over several days a manager delegating with purpose, deadline, standard and one checkpoint, leaving the method to the staff member.

passage: Joseph, you asked how I learned to lead. Sit down. I'm Dolma, and when I was twenty-five I ran the weaving centre in our town near Darjeeling. My first big order was two hundred shawls for a shop in Delhi. I was so frightened I wanted to weave them all myself. My old teacher said, "Give it to your weavers, but tell them everything." So I did. I told Pema and the others the buyer, why the order could save the centre, the date the truck would come, and exactly how tight the weave should be. Then I said, "We'll check the first ten together. After that, weave your way." The truck left on time.

qa.q: How many shawls were in the order?
qa.a: The order was two hundred shawls.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel when the big order came?
qa.a: Dolma felt frightened, wanting to weave all the shawls alone rather than hand them over.

qa.q: Which choice in the story led to the truck leaving on time?
qa.a: Telling the weavers the buyer, the reason, the date and the standard, checking the first ten together, then letting them weave their own way.

qa.q: How might Pema and the other weavers have felt about the order?
qa.a: They likely felt trusted and responsible, knowing why the order mattered and being free to weave their own way after the check.

grounding: An elder recalls delegating a big order with goal, reason, deadline, standard and one check, then trusting the weavers' methods.

passage: The rain started at seven, an hour before sports day, and Rekha's phone buzzed: her brother said Ma's scan had moved to ten, and someone had to take her. Rekha found Disha in the staffroom, shaking out an umbrella. "I need to hand you the whole day," Rekha said. "Goal: every class finishes its events indoors by one. Why: lots of parents took half a day off to watch. Standard: equal turns for each house, first-aid table by the hall door, the little ones go first. How you arrange it is up to you. I'll ring at eleven. Tell me what's working and what isn't." Disha nodded, then began sketching on the back of a timetable. At eleven Rekha called from the hospital corridor. "Relays in the corridor, jumps in the hall," Disha said. "One question: tug-of-war?" "Skip it." By one, the last certificates had been handed out.

qa.q: By what time did every class need to finish its events?
qa.a: By one o'clock.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt handing over sports day at the last minute?
qa.a: Rekha was likely torn and anxious, needed by Ma and by the school at once, but steady enough to trust Disha with a clear plan.

qa.q: Which parts of Rekha's hand-over made it work?
qa.a: She gave the goal, the reason, the standard and a set check-in time, then left the method to Disha, so Disha could plan freely and still ask one question at eleven.

qa.q: What was the day like for Disha?
qa.a: Disha was probably nervous at first but felt trusted, sketched her own plan and ended up running the whole day confidently. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates delegating under pressure by giving the goal, the reason, the deadline and the standard, agreeing a check-in and leaving the method to the other person.
